title: The wooden board
hook: a wooden board struck to call the monks, often inscribed: life and death are grave, time passes swiftly

segments.voice: Yesterday: samu, work as practice, and your line, work is zen. Which chore did you do slowly, all the way to the end? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

Clack. A pause. Clack. Clack. Then faster, and faster, a wooden rattle rolling across the courtyard until it runs out, and stops. Outside a Zen hall there often hangs a thick, heavy board of wood, and someone stands before it with a mallet. The sound tells everyone: come to sit. Walk up close and you may see words brushed on its face. Their message, in plain English: life and death are a great matter. Time passes swiftly. Today: the wooden board.
screen: `CLACK. A PAUSE. CLACK.` → `A BOARD OUTSIDE THE HALL.` → `WORDS ON ITS FACE.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. In Japanese it's called the han: a plank of hard wood hung by cords, struck with a wooden mallet. It calls the community to zazen, and in some places it marks the start of the day's sittings. Its sound isn't musical like a bell. It's dry and blunt, more like a knock on the door than a song. Second, the words. The inscription varies, but the common message, in paraphrase, runs like this: the matter of life and death is great; everything passes, and passes quickly; wake up; don't waste this time. It's not decoration. It's the reason for the sitting, written on the thing that calls you to sit. Third, the board itself wears the message. Struck over and over, day after day, the wood is slowly worn down, and some boards end up with a hollow, or a hole right through the center where the mallet lands. The board is teaching impermanence by being used up. Every strike that calls the monks is also taking a little of the board away. Fourth, why it matters for someone without a board. Time passes swiftly is not a threat. It's a reminder, said plainly, the way a friend might tap your shoulder. In Zen, remembering that life is short isn't meant to make people anxious. It's meant to wake them up to this hour, this breath, this conversation, while it's here. The board doesn't say hurry. It says notice, because this won't come again.
screen: `A PLANK OF WOOD, A MALLET.` · `WORDS: LIFE AND DEATH ARE GREAT.` · `THE BOARD WEARS THROUGH.` · `NOT HURRY. NOTICE.` · then, large: `TIME PASSES SWIFTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Find something you can tap: a table, a book, your own knee. Tap it once, gently, and listen until the sound is completely gone. Breathe. Tap again. Let each tap be a small han: a call back to this moment. Between taps, notice that the last sound has already passed and can't be had again. After a few, stop tapping and simply sit, listening. The bell holds the time.
The wooden board. The han, struck to call a Zen community to sit, and often inscribed with a reminder: life and death are a great matter, time passes swiftly. Today's word.
Your line: time passes swiftly. Today, when you hear a knock, a timer or a door close, let it be a han: stop for one breath and notice this hour. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries and centers a wooden board called the han hangs outside the meditation hall and is struck in a set rhythm to call people to sit; it often carries an inscription about the urgency of life and death and the swift passing of time.

what a scholar hears: the board wears down under the mallet, so the object that announces impermanence slowly shows it.

sources.ref: The han and its inscription (life and death, impermanence)

notes: Inscription paraphrased; wording varies by temple. The common verse runs roughly: great is the matter of birth and death; impermanence is swift; awake, awake; do not waste time. Confirm the paraphrase.
Rhythm (strikes speeding up into a roll) varies by community; described loosely in the hook.
Boards wearing a hollow or a hole through: commonly seen; confirm.
Kanji: 版 is common; some write 板. Confirm the preferred form.
